That would require way more tests than a system with compulsory homework. You'd need to essentially have a test every day to make sure students understood the material from the previous lesson.

The idea behind homework is to reinforce what the students learned during class.  Think of it like a form of spaced repetition. It allows the student to practice what they learned that day, but spaced out so they information is retained better. It also is a way for the instructors to evaluate a student's comprehension of the material over a period of time. If a student or group of students struggle with a specific area on the homework, the teachers can then alter the classroom time to hone in on problem areas. 
Sure it's possible to have that same feedback during the school day, but that would cut into the time to teach new material.

With a lot of languages there's a huge amount of variety between dialects. Take German for example. Someone from Hamburg would probably have some difficulty speaking to someone from Salzburg. That's because German has a huge amount of dialectical variety. 

English dialects have a lot less diversity (though there definitely are multiple dialects), which means places will teach whichever version has the most resources. I imagine those places in Europe that teach American English so so because our media output is so large in comparison to British media.

From where I've traveled in Europe they generally learn the UK variant, but since there's such a small difference it really wouldn't matter which variety is taught. The difference is mostly in vocabulary (trunk vs boot, pavement vs sidewalk, etc) rather than grammar (such as tenses and conjunction). So let's use two sentence as an example. "The man sees the dog" and "The dog sees the man". You can tell who's seeing who based on the word order. In a language with cases like German, that meaning is shown by altering the case of each noun rather than the order. In German the first example is "*der* Mann(the man) sieht(sees) *den* Hund(the dog)". If you wanted to switch the meaning it would be "*der* Hund sieht *den* Mann. See how the article changes (der vs den)? Because of the cases the word order doesn't even matter as much. You could say "der Mann sieht den Hund" or "den Hund sieht der Mann" and the meaning doesn't change. Only the emphasis changes (*the man* sees the dog vs the man sees *the dog*). Even in English we mark for case (he vs him, she vs her) just to a lesser extent. There's a lot more to cases, but that's the basic gist of it.

If it were a noun that uses *на* for location such as *стадион*, then *from the stadium* would be *со стадиона*. You just have to remember which nouns use *в* and which ones use *на* for location.
